sources.title: Transparent loss and guarantee counterexamples
sources.details: For assumed losses [1.2,.8,.6,.7,.9], min=.6 at round3. Hinge max(0,after-before) gives .2 for (.2,.4), zero for (.5,.4): unchanged later quality and worse earlier quality can reduce penalty. With J=L1+L2+lambda*hinge and lambda=1, feasible candidate losses [.001,.002] violate monotonicity but J=.004, lower than nonviolating [1,1] with J=2; a finite soft term alone imposes no hard constraint. Increasing earlier CE by .3 adds .3 to its own unweighted CE term, so per-round CE makes that shortcut costly without proving universal optimality. CE=-log p_gold: binary gold0, [.2,.8] to [.4,.6] lowers CE 1.6094379 to .9162907 while argmax1 stays wrong. A mean drop [1,1] to [0,1.5] does not imply each item improves. Fixed-point counterexample: scalar h_(r+1)=h_r/2 converges to0; a decoder with constant probabilities [.1,.9] for gold0 remains wrong at every state. Thus state convergence does not prove correct answers. No finite training-set observation constrains an arbitrary unobserved input without further assumptions. If validation round3 minimizes loss and round4 maximizes exact-answer accuracy, the stated acceptance metric selects which objective to optimize; neither metric is an algebraic proxy for the other.
